zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check after scan reading: NINJAL, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510; developed by Hideyuki Ohshima with assistance from Taichi Aida, CC BY 4.0 (https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html). The index is an aid, not the authority for this copy's typography or wording.

lines.note: Mairiai describes meeting someone while coming or travelling. The two carons in the principal parts are visible and must not be assimilated to the circumflexes in nearby verbs.

runs.text: alguem. ¶ Item, Vir a tempo alguem de

lines.note: Alguem completes the person encountered on the road. The second sense begins arriving at an opportune time, rather than a second unrelated meaning of the verb.

runs.text: maneira que encontre com o que deſeja, como

lines.note: The timely arrival allows one to encounter what one desires. The examples on the following row specify the occasion; encontre and deſeja belong to the Portuguese explanation.
Mass and preaching exemplify the desired occasion reached in time. The historical spelling and the printed accent in prègação are retained, as is the double-s type in mißa.
Mairiawase means coming upon something by chance. The printed principal parts ſuru and eta are kept rather than recast as a modern conjugation.

runs.text: caſo cõ algũa couſa, como algũa feſta, mißa, &c.

lines.note: Caſo completes a caſo from the preceding row. A feast or mass illustrates the chance encounter; the visible initial c restores como, lost in OCR omo.
Mairikayoi is going and coming, or attending repeatedly. The Portuguese Ir, & vir is a complete gloss; the circumflexed principal parts differ graphically from those in Mairiai.
Mairitsudoi describes people coming together successively. Hũs depois dos begins the Portuguese construction meaning some after the others, continued on the next physical line.
Outros completes hũs depois dos outros, with grande frequencia emphasizing repeated or numerous arrivals. This short continuation belongs to Mairitçudoi, not Mairitçuqi.
Mairitsuki means reaching a destination on coming. Vindo chegar directly matches arrival; the abbreviated u and uita are retained as the printed principal-part endings.
Maisu is a deceiver, explained by hito wo tarasu mono, someone who beguiles people. The Japanese synonym and Portuguese Embaidor identify a person, not the modern counting suffix mai.
Enganador completes the deceptive-person gloss. Maisu wo yuu then illustrates deceptive speech; the Portuguese Embair means to beguile, not to embark or send away.

runs.text: ou enganar falando à võtade muitas couſas.

lines.note: The example concerns deceiving by freely saying many things. À võtade is part of the Portuguese account of the speaker's behaviour; its nasal abbreviation is not expanded.
Mai-sumashi is dancing excellently or completing a dance. The aita principal part reflects the historical inflection and should not be rewritten as modern sumashita.
The alternative sense is finishing the dance. Kokoro mo oyobanu begins an expression meaning beyond imagination; the scan shows bailar with i, not OCR ballar, and a real hyphen after voyo-.
Completes kokoro mo oyobanu hodo mai sumaita: the dance surpassed what one could imagine. Feiq. is the upright source citation; the following book reference is italic.

runs.text: Bailou melhor do que ſe podia imaginar.

lines.note: The Portuguese explicitly says that the person danced better than could be imagined. A visible dotted i supports Bailou rather than OCR Ballou.
Maitan means every morning. Menhaam is retained in its printed historical form, without replacing it by manhaã; the final upright S. marks written usage.
Maiseki is every evening, paraphrased by yuu-sa gotoni. The older Japanese evening expression is coherent here and should not be regularized to a modern yuugata phrase.
Maiseki idete suzumu means going out each evening to enjoy the cool air. The italic Vt introduces the example; ca- begins cada on the following line.
Da completes cada from the previous row. Tomar o freſco explains suzumu as enjoying the cool air, completing the evening-outing example.
Maishuu means every autumn, as aki gotoni and the Portuguese gloss confirm. The scan restores the i in Maixǔ, q in Aqigotoni, and t in todos; these are OCR errors, not historical variants.
Ou cada Outono restates the preceding gloss as each autumn. It continues the same entry and must retain its own physical row.

Maishun means every spring, paraphrased by haru gotoni. The headword visibly contains i. Enlargement confirms the anomalous long ſ in primaſueras; it is preserved instead of silently emending the print to primaueras.
Maiya and yogoto both express every night. The repeated Maiya begins the following example, whose action is keeping a vigil at a temple.
Maiya midou ni tsuya wo mousu describes nightly temple vigils. The printed long-vowel marks and Paſsar spelling are preserved; the Portuguese object continues on the next line.
Noites vigiando no templo completes the explanation as spending the nights keeping watch in a temple. This is the conclusion of Maiya, not part of the following wind-name entry.

runs.text: Vento ſul. No Ximo ſe diz,

lines.note: Maje denotes the south wind. The j descends below the line, unlike OCR Maie; the explanation gives Faye no caje as the Ximo regional expression. Ximo occurs within the Portuguese sentence.
No caje completes Faye no caje, the regional name of the south wind. This Japanese continuation belongs to the preceding gloss rather than constituting an independent entry.
Maje, mazuru, mazeta gives the verb to mix. It is a separate homographic entry from the wind-name above; the Portuguese Misturar makes the distinction explicit.
Mazemono is a mixture or mixed material. The gloss begins Miſtura, with a visible u rather than OCR a, and continues its description after the conjunction.
Misturada completes couſa confuſa, & misturada: something confused or mixed together. The single-word continuation remains a separate physical line.
Maji and majii are equated with mai and described as a negative-future particle. The lowercase l introduces an alternative; fu continues as futuro without a visible terminal hyphen.
Turo completes futuro. The compiler contrasts conversational maji/majii with majiqi for writing; this is the dictionary's grammatical characterization, not an editorial modernization.

Eſcritura completes the written-register explanation. Arumajii koto no aru wa kiquaina koto ja then begins an example about something seemingly impossible occurring; qi- belongs to the divided adjective.
Quaina completes qiquaina, strange or extraordinary. The Portuguese begins explaining the occurrence of something that appears impossible, with the abbreviated q̃ left unexpanded.

runs.text: poßiuel he couſa duuidoſa, & que não ſe en-

lines.note: Poßiuel completes impoßiuel from the previous row. Duuidoſa describes the event as doubtful or puzzling; both words are visibly recoverable from OCR piſtiuel and diuidoſa, without modernizing their historical spellings.
Tende completes entende, concluding that the puzzling event is not understood. This short fragment is body text and closes the grammatical example.
Majinai denotes charms or incantations. The Portuguese labels them prayers and non-Christian ceremonies; that religious assessment belongs to the historical dictionary, not to the reviewer.
Cas completes gentilicas. Feitiçarias adds sorcery or magical practices as the alternative gloss, completing the noun entry before the cognate verb.
Majinai is now the verb for performing the charms or prayers just described. The scan has a caron on ǒ but no corresponding mark on ota; the latter is not silently regularized.

runs.text: Canto do olho da parte de fora antre as

lines.note: Majiri here names the outer corner of the eye. The Portuguese locates it between the upper and lower lash lines, rather than referring to mixture as in the later homograph.

The reference to the two eyelids or lash lines completes the outer-corner definition. Magaxira names the other corner of the eye; it is a Japanese contrasting term, not embedded Portuguese vocabulary.
Tro completes outro: Magaxira is the other, inner corner of the eye. The short row concludes the anatomical comparison.

Majiri is a mixture, and majiri wo nasu means to mix. Both occurrences visibly begin Majiri, correcting OCR Mairi and Najiriuo. The weak terminal mark after Mi is retained as the baseline hyphen; its precise shape remains uncertain.
ſturar completes Miſturar from the preceding row, translating majiri wo nasu. The fragment remains in place rather than being joined into an artificial single line.
Majiri, majiru, majitta is the intransitive verb for becoming mixed. The example begins aoba, green leaves, and continues at the top of column 2; OCR Najiri misread the initial M.

Continues Auoba- from the bottom of column 1: late cherry blossoms mingled with green leaves. Hatsuhana yori mo introduces a comparison with the first blossoms; the wording is a quoted example, not a new entry.
Mezzuraxuu completes the comparison as more remarkable or worth seeing. Feiq. cites the Heike source in upright type; the Portuguese translation begins As flores across the line break.

runs.text: res da cereijeira que vem tarde misturadas com

lines.note: The late-arriving cherry blossoms are described as mixed with something, specified below as green leaves. The scan supports the u in misturadas, correcting OCR mistaradas without changing the provisional st allograph.

runs.text: as folhas verdes, he mais pera ver q̃ aspri-

lines.note: The flowers mixed with green leaves are more worth seeing than the first flowers. The small printed q̃ supplies the comparison omitted by OCR; the tight aspri- spacing is retained.
Meiras completes primeiras, the first blossoms in the comparison. This short row closes the example begun at the end of column 1.
Majirou is an adverb meaning clearly, equated with meihaku ni. The Japanese gloss requires f, and the scan shows its cross-stroke: OCR Meiſacuni was a meaningful f/long-s confusion.
Majiroi is the adjective clear, paraphrased by akirakana or meihakuna. The lowercase l means or; the Portuguese noun couſa is divided across the line boundary.
ſa completes couſa clara, a clear thing. This physical continuation belongs to the adjective Majiroi, not the blinking verb that follows.
Majiroqi gives the verb for blinking or opening and closing the eyes. Enlargement recovers jiro in the headword instead of OCR Maitoqi; the principal part oita remains as printed.
Lhos completes olhos, followed by peſtenejar, to blink. The alternative Portuguese verb confirms the eye-movement sense and the Japanese headword recovery.
Majita is the space below the eyes. The repeated Majitauo begins the example about looking downward, helping distinguish the headword from superficially similar eye terms nearby.

runs.text: Olhar com os olhos pera baixo.

lines.note: Miru completes majita wo miru, explained as directing the eyes downward. The Portuguese phrase belongs to the example rather than introducing another sense.
Majiwari denotes mixing or association. Majiwari wo fukou suru begins the example of deepening a relationship; the scan supplies the t omitted in OCR Miſura.

runs.text: Ter ẽtre ſi grãde amizade, l

lines.note: ſuru completes the example: to have a close friendship or alliance with one another. The printed l introduces the alternative liança; neither nasal abbreviation is expanded.
Majiwari wo nasu supplies the sexual sense, glossed as having carnal intercourse. It is an illustrative phrase under the same noun, not a separate conjugated headword.
Majiwari, majiwaru, majiwatta gives the verb to mingle. Xequẽ- begins seken, the worldly or social sphere, with an abbreviation tilde rather than an extra long-vowel mark.
No chiri ni majiwaru completes the image of mingling with the dust of the world. The Portuguese begins mixing or moving among something, continued by the next row.

runs.text: dar de miſtura com as couſas vãas do mundo.

lines.note: Dar completes andar. The gloss explains mingling with the vain things of the world, preserving the source's moral characterization and its vãas spelling.
Tanin ni majiwaru means associating with other people. The scan reads Tanin ni, not OCR Taninini; its word division and the Portuguese social sense agree.
Tros completes outros from the preceding example. Fuufu ni majiwaru then gives marital intercourse; the mark over u is read as a caron after comparison with nearby caroned forms.
Matrimonial completes copula matrimonial, specifying intercourse within marriage. It concludes the last example under the verb majiwaru.
Majiye is the noun mixing or mixture. The Portuguese Miſtura is complete on this row and distinguishes the noun from the following verb entry.
Majiye, majiyuru, majiyeta gives the transitive verb to mix. The quotation starts with the shore and mountains; ya- continues into yama on the next physical line.
The shore and mountain storm mingle their sounds with one another. Fibiqiuo represents hibiki wo, sound or resonance, and the printed majiyete is retained rather than modernized.

runs.text: Lib. 27. As ondas da praya, & o

lines.note: Taif. is the upright source label, followed by an italic reference to book 27, not OCR book 2. The Portuguese begins translating the shore imagery as waves on the beach.
The mountain wind completes the paired sounds in the quotation; miſturandoſe explains their mingling. The compiler's rendering need not be forced into a word-for-word match with the Japanese imagery.

Majut denotes magical arts, explained as a tengu's extraordinary powers. The Portuguese calls the effect a demon's work or marvel; the final t is a historical checked-coda spelling, not an omitted tçu.
Vilha completes marauilha. Majut wo okonou is practising those magical arts; the final caron and the attached object particle in Majutuo are retained as printed.

runs.text: Fazer couſas que parecem milagres por arte do

lines.note: The gloss describes doing things that seem miraculous through the agency named below. Parecem is one printed word; the OCR's pare cem introduced a false internal boundary.
Demonio completes por arte do demonio. This is the historical compiler's religious explanation of magic, not a new entry or an independent claim by the reviewer.
Mama means a manner or condition. Sono mama de wa narumai begins the example that something cannot be done or remain in that manner; the word mama is divided at the physical line end.
Madeua completes sono mama de wa, followed by the negative narumai. The Portuguese says it cannot be that way and divides maneira at the line boundary.
Neira completes maneira. Nozomi no mama ni then expresses following one's desire; the Portuguese A võtade begins across this row and the next.
Tade completes võtade, with conforme ao deſejo restating conformity to one's wish. This closes the first Mama entry before the room-by-room sense.
Mama here means each room, distinct from manner or inclination. Mamani fiuo begins the instruction to light a fire or lamp in each room.
Toboite voqe completes the instruction to have lamps lit. The historical toboite form is not corrected to a modern toboshi-te form; the Portuguese specifies a lighted lamp.
Cada camara completes the room-by-room instruction. Zaxiqui is a Japanese room-name embedded in the Portuguese explanation and is retained with its visible italic styling.
Mamachichi means stepfather. The single-word Portuguese gloss Padrasto is complete and begins a sequence of step-family terms.
Mamaco means stepchild or stepson, here glossed Enteado. It is an independent entry within the step-family sequence.
Mamafaua is the printed form for stepmother. Its internal faua spelling is preserved rather than replaced by a modern Japanese or romanized form.
Mamamusume is specifically a stepdaughter, matched by filha enteada. The internal long ſ belongs to the Japanese headword's printed spelling.
Mamana is illustrated by waga mamana koto wo suru, doing things according to one's own wishes. The example supplies the usage directly rather than a separate Portuguese headword definition.

runs.text: Fazer as couſas como hũ quer, ou à ſua võtade.

lines.note: The Portuguese translates the example as doing things as one wishes or at one's own will. The wording is about self-directed conduct; the abbreviated nasal forms are retained.
Mamani means in accordance with. Okonomi no mama ni mouse begins an instruction to say something in the way one prefers; ni is on the following physical line.
Ni mǒxe completes the Japanese instruction. Mon. is the upright citation label; the Portuguese Dizeilho como quiſerdes says to tell it as one wishes, retaining the historical spelling.
Mamatete is another word for stepfather, with the same Portuguese meaning as Mamachichi above. The repeated gloss does not make this a duplicate line to remove.
Mame is a bean or pulse, here described as Japanese beans or grains. This is a complete body entry; the separate Mame catchword below anticipates the different blister sense on f304.
